design_detail: Narrative overview published as an RTI Press occasional paper (Methods Report, November 2016), which the authors say is written for the educated layperson and for policy makers. No search method, selection criteria or appraisal. Sections: medicinal cannabis use, an overview of edibles (what they are, sales, survey prevalence, perceptions), the ‘promises’ of edibles, the ‘challenges’ of edibles (onset and duration, dose, children, visitors, labelling), and the rules for edibles in the four US states with legal retail sales in 2016 (Alaska, Colorado, Oregon, Washington). Sources range from laboratory studies of oral THC and of medicines containing it, through poison-centre data, a hospital letter and a state sales report, to news reports, state regulations and a conference paper.
can_establish: How the questions about edibles were framed in 2016 and which primary sources the authors drew on: the pharmacology they cite for the slower onset and longer duration after eating THC than after inhaling it (first-pass conversion to the active metabolite 11-OH-THC, the cited onset and peak times, low oral bioavailability); the variability of THC content and the problems of labelling (reported second-hand); and the state of regulation in four states in 2016. It points to primary studies that can then be read.
cannot_establish: Anything new: it has no data of its own. It cannot show how common harms from edibles are or how they compare with other routes. Its statement that eating cannabis does not seem to affect lung function or cancer risk is the authors’ inference from the premise that harm comes from smoke; no study of people who eat cannabis is cited for it. Its statement that edibles account for most health-care visits for cannabis intoxication comes from a 2015 viewpoint (not read) and conflicts with later hospital counts (Monte 2019: 115 of 762 intoxication visits, 15.1%). The figure that 65 percent of medicinal cannabis patients had severe impairment comes from a conference paper by three RTI authors and does not match the reference list as cited. The label-accuracy result (83 percent of tested products more than 10 percent from the label) is reported second-hand from a paper that has not yet been read for this library (Vandrey 2015).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative overview). No search, database, date range or inclusion criteria are given; the Introduction says the authors critically examine extant research and blend science and regulatory factors (Introduction, paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated. The Introduction says the discussion focuses on consequences of intentional use of edibles in adults, although several paragraphs on children’s exposures follow (Challenges of Edibles, 10th and 11th paragraphs).
sample.selection_effects: The authors chose the sources, and there is no way to see what was left out. Cited work is mostly from before 2016 and mostly from the United States; several cited items are not peer-reviewed studies (a newspaper investigation, a children’s hospital figure reported through a hospital association web item, a commissioned market report, a conference presentation).

exposure.measurement: None of its own. The cited exposures are edible THC products and, for comparison, smoked, vaporized or intravenous THC and oral medicines containing THC (dronabinol, nabiximols).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As cited: inhaled THC takes initial effect within minutes, peaks in about 20 to 30 minutes and tapers off within 2 to 3 hours; eaten THC takes initial effect after 30 to 90 minutes, gives a longer-lasting high and peaks 2 to 4 hours after ingestion (Grotenhermen 2003, as cited); oral bioavailability is 6 to 10 percent of the amount in the product (Schwilke 2009, as cited); in Cone 1988 (brownies) peak responses averaged about 3 hours and effects dissipated within 24 hours (as described). State rules in 2016 defined a serving as no more than 10 mg of THC and, in Colorado and Washington, capped a recreational product at 100 mg of THC.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, apart from the confounding of cannabis smoking by tobacco smoking in the epidemiology of lung cancer (Promises of Edibles, 11th paragraph).

comparison.controls: Not applicable (no data of its own). Comparators in the cited work are smoked and intravenous THC (Hollister 1981), smoked cannabis and placebo (Cone 1988, Cooper 2013), dronabinol, and, for the lung argument, tobacco smoke.

outcomes.instruments: None of its own. The outcomes in the cited work are subjective drug-effect ratings, plasma THC and 11-OH-THC, counts of poison-centre calls and emergency visits, and THC content measured against the label.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. Figures it quotes from other sources, all second-hand: 1.96 million medicinal and 2.85 million retail edible units sold in Colorado in 2014, said to be about 45 percent of total cannabis sales in the state (a state report; the measure of sales is not stated); 29.8 percent of US adults who had ever used cannabis reported eating or drinking it (Schauer 2016); poison-centre calls about cannabis rose 30.3 percent a year in decriminalized states, 11.5 percent in states in transition and 1.5 percent in states without legal change, 2005 to 2011 (Wang 2014); a Colorado children’s hospital emergency department saw no accidental edible ingestions in 2005 to 2009, eight children in 2013 and 14 in 2014 (Baskfield 2015); emergency visits by out-of-state patients after edibles at an Aurora, Colorado hospital rose from 85 to 168 per 10,000 visits between 2013 and 2014 (Kim 2016); 83 percent of medicinal edibles tested in California and Washington differed from the labelled THC by more than 10 percent (Vandrey 2015); 65 percent of medicinal cannabis patients reported severe impairment (conference paper).
analysis.selective_reporting: Not assessable: with no search method there is no way to know what was left out.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The paper has no results of its own. It collates cited studies and reports: eaten THC acts later and for longer than inhaled THC (cited pharmacology), with an active liver metabolite that is higher after eating; the THC content of edibles is often inexact against the label (second-hand); poison-centre and hospital counts of child and visitor exposures rose in Colorado and other states after policy changes; one death after an edible is described; and the four states with legal retail sales regulated edibles differently in 2016.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that the most prominent difference between eating and inhaling cannabis extracts is the delayed onset, that consumers may take more than they intend before the effect arrives, often with profoundly adverse effects, and that little research has compared ingestion with other routes. The body goes further than its sources: it says eating edibles does not seem to affect lung function or raise cancer risk, “a solid rationale for choosing this route”, although no study of people who eat cannabis is cited; it says edible products are responsible for the majority of health-care visits for cannabis intoxication, citing a viewpoint; and the Conclusions call additional regulation evident given the frequency of overdoses and accidental child exposures, without counting either.

timeline.event: Brownie study in people with cannabis experience (Cone et al.), as described by the authors; not read.

Label testing of edible medicinal cannabis products in California and Washington (Vandrey et al.), cited here second-hand for 83 percent of products differing from the label by more than 10 percent. Not yet readable for this library; will be added.

Chart review of cannabis-related emergency visits by route at one Colorado hospital: edible-attributed visits were 115 of 762 intoxication visits (15.1%), against this overview’s statement that edibles account for most visits for intoxication.
Children’s edible exposures 2017 to 2021 (Tweet et al.), later data on the child-poisoning concern raised here. Not yet readable for this library; will be added.

replication.where_it_stands: A 2016 overview, now dated. Primary studies from after 2016 (Monte 2019 in this batch; Tweet 2023 and Vandrey 2015 once added) are better sources for numbers. Its description of the timing of eaten and inhaled THC is the same cited review (Grotenhermen 2003) that the 2019 hospital paper’s Discussion uses.

funding.funder: RTI International internal funds and National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) grant DA-03672 (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the author manuscript; the author-information panel gives affiliations only. No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are declared.
funding.affiliations_note: All eight authors are at RTI International (laboratory, economics, policy, epidemiology and behavioural pharmacology staff, per the author notes), and the paper appears in the institute’s own RTI Press series. Three of them (Novak, Peiper, Wiley) are the authors of the conference paper that is the source of the 65 percent figure. The opinion-like passages (the lung and cancer rationale; the need for more regulation) are the authors’ views. Recorded as a reason to read closely, not to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Studies that count people rather than sales or visits: people who eat cannabis products and people who inhale it, with amounts and product content measured, followed for harms, including lung and cancer outcomes in people who eat cannabis and do not smoke tobacco or cannabis; independent testing of label accuracy across brands, states and years; and multi-hospital emergency data by route.

domains.note: No search, dates or selection criteria; the authors chose the evidence, and what was left out cannot be seen.

No formal appraisal. Some limits are named (sales data do not show how many people eat edibles; the literature on cannabis-induced psychosis is limited; the accuracy of common perceptions about edibles has not been scientifically evaluated), but sources of very different strength are used side by side: laboratory studies, case reports, a newspaper investigation, a children’s hospital association web item, a conference paper and a viewpoint.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The 65 percent severe-impairment figure comes from a conference paper by Novak, Peiper and Wiley, all three authors of this overview, and the in-text citation does not match the reference list. Otherwise the authors’ own work is not prominent.

Some inferences are hedged (the liver metabolite “may be responsible” for the stronger effect; the entourage idea is attributed to “some scientists”), but others are stated as findings: eating does not seem to affect lung function or cancer risk, with no study of people who eat cannabis; edible products are responsible for the majority of intoxication visits; the need for more regulation is evident.

domains.domain: Balance of promises and challenges of edibles
domains.note: The promises (discretion, longer action, avoiding smoke) rest mainly on perception and inference, and the authors say the accuracy of those perceptions has not been scientifically evaluated; the challenges rest on a mix of pharmacology, case reports, poison-centre and hospital counts and news. The confounding of cannabis-smoke epidemiology by tobacco is noted. No data compare harms of eating with harms of other routes.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative overview (METHODS §5.3 lists none), and this one is written for lay readers and policy makers. It is open about its purpose and flags some limits, and its descriptive points (delayed onset, variable labelling, state rules) can be traced to cited sources. But it has no search or selection method, leans on second-hand reports and a conference paper, states some inferences as findings, and makes one statement (edibles responsible for most intoxication visits) that later hospital counts do not support. Use it to see how the issues were framed in 2016 and to locate primary sources; cite the primary studies, not this overview, for any number.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC5260817 (author manuscript; abstract, all sections, acknowledgments, author notes, legal citations and reference list read as text; no tables or figures; no conflict-of-interest statement in the manuscript)

key_findings.finding: The overview is written for the educated layperson and policy makers and concentrates on intentional use of edibles by adults. Its abstract says the most prominent difference between eating and inhaling cannabis extracts is the delayed onset with eating, and that little research has evaluated how ingestion differs from other methods in efficacy, subjective effects and safety.

Colorado sold 1.96 million medicinal and 2.85 million retail edible units in 2014, said to be about 45 percent of total cannabis sales in the state (a state report). The authors note that homemade edibles are not tracked, that sales do not show how many people eat edibles, and that how many retail edibles were used by the purchaser is unknown.
key_findings.note: The measure of ‘total cannabis sales’ is not stated; compare Monte 2019, where edibles were 0.32% of THC sold by weight.

key_findings.finding: In a US national survey, 29.8 percent of adults who had ever used cannabis reported eating or drinking it (Schauer 2016, as cited); surveys in several US states and Canada found that 11 to 26 percent of medicinal cannabis patients had eaten an edible in their lifetime.

Perceptions attributed to people who choose edibles (discreet and convenient, a calmer high, avoiding the toxins of smoking) are described as anecdotal; the authors say scientific evaluation of their accuracy is incomplete.

Few laboratory studies used real edibles. In Cone 1988 (brownies, people with cannabis experience) peak responses averaged about 3 hours after ingestion and effects dissipated within 24 hours, while pulse, blood pressure and pupil dilation did not differ from placebo (as described). Hollister 1981 (a cookie) found a longer-lasting and less intoxicating effect than smoked or intravenous THC (as described).
key_findings.note: Both studies are described second-hand and not read.

key_findings.finding: On smoke: cannabis and tobacco smoke seem similar in toxicity in kind (both contain toxins and carcinogens); cannabis smoke is linked to lung inflammation and bronchitis; the link to chronic lung disease is unclear; epidemiological research links habitual smoking to several cancers but is complicated by small samples and co-occurring tobacco smoking. The authors then write that eating edibles does not seem to affect lung function or raise cancer risk, a solid rationale for choosing the route.
key_findings.note: No study of people who eat cannabis is cited for the last sentence; it is an inference.

key_findings.finding: After eating, liver first-pass metabolism produces 11-OH-THC, a potent psychoactive metabolite that appears in blood in higher quantities than after inhaling; the authors write that it may be responsible for the stronger and longer-lasting effect of edibles compared with comparable doses of smoked cannabis.

Inhaled THC takes initial effect within minutes, peaks in about 20 to 30 minutes and tapers off within 2 to 3 hours; eaten THC takes initial effect after 30 to 90 minutes and gives a longer-lasting high with a peak 2 to 4 hours after ingestion; weight, metabolism, sex and eating habits affect how soon and how long (Grotenhermen 2003 and others, as cited).

After oral doses, plasma THC is lower than after smoking or infusion and how closely it tracks intoxication varies widely across people (Hollister 1981, as cited); oral bioavailability is 6 to 10 percent of the amount in the product (Schwilke 2009, as cited). The authors say inconsistency and delayed intoxication may lead both new and experienced people to take more than intended, and that edible products are responsible for the majority of health-care visits due to cannabis intoxication (a 2015 viewpoint, not read).
key_findings.note: Compare Monte 2019: 115 of 762 intoxication visits (15.1%) were edible-attributed.

key_findings.finding: Poison-centre calls about cannabis rose 30.3 percent a year in decriminalized states, 11.5 percent a year in states in transition and 1.5 percent a year in states without legal change, 2005 to 2011 (Wang 2014); a later review found similar increases in edible-related calls in 2013 to 2015 (Cao 2016). A Colorado children’s hospital emergency department saw no accidental edible ingestions in 2005 to 2009, eight children in 2013 and 14 in 2014; the authors write that emergency visits from child exposure remain relatively low.
key_findings.note: Cited second-hand; the hospital figures come from a hospital association web article.

key_findings.finding: Emergency visits by out-of-state patients at an Aurora, Colorado hospital for problems after edibles almost doubled, from 85 to 168 per 10,000 visits between 2013 and 2014, with no significant change for Colorado residents (Kim 2016, as cited); that study’s authors attributed the rise to higher potency and visitors’ unfamiliarity with edibles.

One death after an edible is described: a 19-year-old man who jumped from a fourth-floor balcony in Colorado in March 2014 after eating a cannabis cookie; the autopsy named cannabis intoxication a chief contributing factor (a public-health case report in the CDC’s weekly report, as cited); the text adds that, having not felt intoxicated within 60 minutes of a first serving, he ate the whole cookie within 2 hours of that serving.

Severe cannabis-induced behavioural impairment is said to be common, experienced by 65 percent of medicinal cannabis patients, while no deaths have been directly attributed to the acute physical toxicity of cannabis. Psychotic symptoms after overconsumption usually last for the duration of intoxication and in some cases up to several days; the authors say many reported cases of cannabis-induced psychosis follow ingestion of an edible (case reports).
key_findings.note: The 65 percent figure is cited to a source that does not match the reference list (see reporting issues); the statement that many cases follow edibles rests on case reports with no denominator.

key_findings.finding: Labelling: a 2014 newspaper investigation found the THC content of retail edibles often differed significantly from the label; from mid-2014 Colorado required THC to be tested and labelled but tested only against a threshold, which does not check label accuracy. One study of medicinal edibles in California and Washington found that 83 percent differed from the labelled THC by more than 10 percent, with over half containing significantly less and nearly a quarter significantly more (Vandrey 2015, as described).
key_findings.note: Second-hand; Vandrey 2015 not yet readable for this library and will be added.

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: many questions remain unanswered about the basic effects of edibles and how consumers understand and use them; further research is needed; the need for additional regulation is said to be evident given the frequency of overdoses and accidental child exposures (neither counted).
key_findings.note: The regulatory conclusion is the authors’ policy view.

reporting_issues.issue: The 65 percent figure for severe impairment is cited in the text as Novak, Peiper and Wenger (2015); the reference list has Novak, Peiper and Wiley (2016), a paper presented at a 2016 drug-dependence meeting on a daily-diary study of medical cannabis patients.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure cannot be traced to a published study, and all three authors of the meeting paper are authors of the overview. It concerns medicinal cannabis in general, not edibles.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that edible products are responsible for the majority of health-care visits due to cannabis intoxication cites a 2015 viewpoint (not read). A later chart review of 2012 to 2016 visits at one Colorado hospital (Monte 2019) found 115 of 762 intoxication visits (15.1%) were edible-attributed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement should not be cited as established; the counts and limits of Monte 2019 are the better source.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion that eating edibles does not seem to affect lung function or raise cancer risk, giving a solid rationale for choosing the route, has no cited study of people who eat cannabis.
reporting_issues.consequence: An inference from the premise that harm comes from smoke; an absence of studies is not evidence of no harm.

reporting_issues.issue: About 45 percent of total cannabis sales in Colorado in 2014 is attributed to edible units, but the measure of sales (units, revenue or THC weight) is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Shares of sales differ greatly by measure (Monte 2019 puts edibles at 0.32% of THC sold by weight), so the 45 percent cannot be set against hospital counts.
